This declaration defines the named export `limitFunction`. Its `function_` parameter is declared as `(...arguments_: Arguments) => PromiseLike<ReturnType>`, and its `options` parameter is declared as `Options`. Its declared return type is an intersection of the callable `(...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>` with `Pick<LimitFunction, 'clearQueue' | 'onIdle'>`. The declaration does not establish the runtime behavior of the returned callable, only the declared type-level contract.

# p-limit

> Run multiple promise-returning & async functions with limited concurrency

*Works in Node.js and browsers.*

## Install

```sh
npm install p-limit
```

## Usage

```js
import pLimit from 'p-limit';

const limit = pLimit(1);

const input = [
	limit(() => fetchSomething('foo')),
	limit(() => fetchSomething('bar')),
	limit(() => doSomething())
];

// Only one promise is run at once
const result = await Promise.all(input);
console.log(result);
```

## API

### pLimit(concurrency) <sup>default export</sup>

Returns a `limit` function.

#### concurrency

Type: `number | object`\
Minimum: `1`

Concurrency limit.

You can pass a number or an options object with a `concurrency` property.

#### rejectOnClear

Type: `boolean`\
Default: `false`

Reject pending promises with an `AbortError` when `clearQueue()` is called.
This is recommended if you await the returned promises, for example with `Promise.all`, so pending tasks do not remain unresolved after `clearQueue()`.

```js
import pLimit from 'p-limit';

const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1});
```

### limit(fn, ...args)

Returns the promise returned by calling `fn(...args)`.

#### fn

Type: `Function`

Promise-returning/async function.

#### args

Any arguments to pass through to `fn`.

Support for passing arguments on to the `fn` is provided in order to be able to avoid creating unnecessary closures. You probably don't need this optimization unless you're pushing a *lot* of functions.

Warning: Avoid calling the same `limit` function inside a function that is already limited by it. This can create a deadlock where inner tasks never run. Use a separate limiter for inner tasks.

### limit.map(iterable, mapperFunction)

Process an iterable of inputs with limited concurrency.

The mapper function receives the item value and its index.

Returns a promise equivalent to `Promise.all(Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index)))`.

If the iterable throws during iteration, the returned promise rejects with that error. Mapper functions that were already scheduled still run, and their results are discarded.

This is a convenience function for processing inputs that arrive in batches. For more complex use cases, see [p-map](https://github.com/sindresorhus/p-map).

### limit.activeCount

The number of promises that are currently running.

### limit.pendingCount

The number of promises that are waiting to run (i.e. their internal `fn` was not called yet).

### limit.clearQueue()

Discard pending promises that are waiting to run.

This might be useful if you want to tear down the queue at the end of your program's lifecycle or discard any function calls referencing an intermediary state of your app.

Note: This does not cancel promises that are already running.

When `rejectOnClear` is enabled, pending promises are rejected with an `AbortError`.
This is recommended if you await the returned promises, for example with `Promise.all`, so pending tasks do not remain unresolved after `clearQueue()`.

### limit.concurrency

Get or set the concurrency limit.

### limitFunction(fn, options) <sup>named export</sup>

Returns a function with limited concurrency.

The returned function manages its own concurrent executions, allowing you to call it multiple times without exceeding the specified concurrency limit.

Ideal for scenarios where you need to control the number of simultaneous executions of a single function, rather than managing concurrency across multiple functions.

```js
import {limitFunction} from 'p-limit';

const limitedFunction = limitFunction(async () => {
	return doSomething();
}, {concurrency: 1});

const input = Array.from({length: 10}, limitedFunction);

// Only one promise is run at once.
await Promise.all(input);
```

#### fn

Type: `Function`

Promise-returning/async function.

#### options

Type: `object`

#### concurrency

Type: `number`\
Minimum: `1`

Concurrency limit.

#### rejectOnClear

Type: `boolean`\
Default: `false`

Reject pending promises with an `AbortError` when `clearQueue()` is called.
This is recommended if you await the returned promises, for example with `Promise.all`, so pending tasks do not remain unresolved after `clearQueue()`.

### limitedFunction.clearQueue()

Discard pending calls that have not started yet.

When `rejectOnClear` is enabled, pending promises are rejected with an `AbortError`. Otherwise, their promises remain unresolved.

This does not cancel calls that are already running.

## Recipes

See [recipes.md](recipes.md) for common use cases and patterns.

## FAQ

### How is this different from the [`p-queue`](https://github.com/sindresorhus/p-queue) package?

This package is only about limiting the number of concurrent executions, while `p-queue` is a fully featured queue implementation with lots of different options, introspection, and ability to pause the queue.

## Related

- [p-throttle](https://github.com/sindresorhus/p-throttle) - Throttle promise-returning & async functions
- [p-debounce](https://github.com/sindresorhus/p-debounce) - Debounce promise-returning & async functions
- [p-map](https://github.com/sindresorhus/p-map) - Run promise-returning & async functions concurrently with different inputs
- [p-all](https://github.com/sindresorhus/p-all) - Run promise-returning & async functions concurrently with optional limited concurrency
- [More…](https://github.com/sindresorhus/promise-fun)

Observed source excerpt from "index.d.ts":

```text

	options: Options
```

Now let me think through the design carefully.

## Design analysis

**Requirements for `onIdle(): Promise<void>`:**
1. Resolves when both running/reserved slots and waiting queue are empty.
2. Already idle call resolves normally.
3. Multiple waiters work, including rejected jobs.
4. `clearQueue` must release waiters when queue empty and no jobs active, even when discarded promises stay unresolved under `rejectOnClear:false`.
5. Reserved slots count as active.
6. Resolving a job that enqueues another job must not report idle early.
7. Preserve FIFO and concurrency changes.

Let me examine the internals. `activeCount` is incremented in `resumeNext` (when a job is dequeued and `run` scheduled) or in `enqueue`. Wait — look carefully:

- `enqueue` creates a promise, queues the item, and if `activeCount < concurrency` calls `resumeNext()`. But `resumeNext` requires `queue.size > 0`, and increments activeCount. So an immediate job increments activeCount there. Good.
- `activeCount` decrements in `next()` after the job's result settles.

**"Reserved slots count as active"** — a job is "reserved" once it has been dequeued/scheduled (activeCount incremented) but its `run` hasn't actually started executing yet? Actually the `run` is scheduled via `.then(...)`, so there's a microtask gap. During that gap, activeCount>0 but no user function running. `onIdle` must wait for these too.

**"resolving a job that enqueues another job must not report idle early"** — Consider: job A resolves. In `run`, after `await result`, it calls `next()` which decrements activeCount and calls `resumeNext()`. But the user's function may have enqueued a new job during its execution. The new job sits in the queue, so `queue.size>0`, so we're not idle. But consider a subtle case: A resolves synchronously-ish; `next()` decrements to 0 and calls `resumeNext()`. If a new job was enqueued *by the resolving job* but processed... hmm. Actually the concern is ordering of the idle check relative to `resumeNext` draining the queue. Let me design a robust checker.

Let me define idle as: `activeCount === 0 && queue.size === 0`. A `checkIdle()` is called after any transition that could lead to idle: in `next()` after decrement+resumeNext, in `clearQueue`, and at `enqueue` (no). Waiters stored in an array; when idle, flush all.

But the tricky part: microtask/timing. When a job's promise resolves, `run`'s `await result` continuation is a microtask. `onIdle()` called right after the job resolves but before `next()` runs would see activeCount=1, so not idle, and it registers a waiter. Good — `next()` later flushes it. 

The "resolving a job that enqueues another job must not report idle early" case: A's function resolves and, inside itself before resolving, enqueues B. Sequence:
- A's function returns (resolves result), during execution it called `limit(B)` → enqueue B, activeCount is at concurrency so B queued.
- `run` await result continuation → `next()`: activeCount-- , `resumeNext()` dequeues B, activeCount++, schedules B's run.
- Then checkIdle: activeCount=1 (B reserved) → not idle. Good.

But what if the resolving job enqueues B in a `.then` attached to its own promise *after* p-limit's `run` continuation? Ordering matters. The requirement is specifically that we must not report idle early. The safest approach: check idle in `checkIdle()` only when `activeCount===0 && queue.size===0`, and call it from `next()` *after* `resumeNext()`. Since `resumeNext` synchronously increments activeCount for a dequeued job, that's covered.

Now **clearQueue releasing waiters under rejectOnClear:false**: `clearQueue` empties the queue. Discarded promises stay unresolved (their resolve/reject never called). If no jobs active, we must release onIdle waiters → call checkIdle after clearing.

Let me also think: should `onIdle` be exposed on `limitFunction`? Yes: "on a limiter and its limitFunction wrapper."

**Type declarations**: add `onIdle: () => Promise<void>` to `LimitFunction`, and add to the limitFunction return `Pick<LimitFunction, 'clearQueue' | 'onIdle'>`.

Let me now write the implementation. I'll add a `idleWaiters` array and `flushIdleWaiters`, plus `checkIdle`. To make waiters robust against rejected jobs, the resolution of onIdle doesn't depend on job outcomes at all—it only depends on counts.

Let me consider whether `checkIdle` should be called anywhere else so that a waiter registered while idle is handled. `onIdle()` itself: if already idle, resolve immediately; else push waiter. There's a race: a waiter registered when not idle, and the transition to idle happens synchronously... no, JS is single threaded; if onIdle runs and sees not idle, the transition will happen in a future microtask/task which will call checkIdle. But could the transition have already "logically" happened without checkIdle being called? Every path that can zero both counts must call checkIdle. Paths:
- `next()` → after decrement and resumeNext.
- `clearQueue()` → after clearing.
- `run` is where next is called. Also the `run` scheduled via `.then` — if between enqueue and run the queue is cleared... activeCount already incremented, so not idle until run finishes.
- concurrency setter's microtask calls resumeNext; that can only increase activeCount or leave queue. If queue becomes empty via resumeNext, activeCount>0. Fine.

One more: `next()` calls `resumeNext()` which may dequeue and increment activeCount, so checkIdle after is correct.

But consider `activeCount` transition to zero where there's still a pending `queueItem` whose internal promise `.then(run)` hasn't fired but activeCount was already counted. Actually activeCount counts it, so we wait. Good — "reserved slots count as active."

Let me implement now.

There's a subtle issue with the "enqueue another job" test. Let me trace it:

`second` is the running job at concurrency 1. Inside it, `limit(() => {enqueued=true})` is called — but at that moment `activeCount` is 1, so it's queued. Then second's function returns. `next()` decrements to 0, `resumeNext()` dequeues the enqueued job, increments to 1. `flushIdleWaiters` sees activeCount=1, no flush. Good.

But wait — in my test, the enqueued job is enqueued *inside* second's function body. `second`'s async function calls `limit(...)` synchronously then returns. Fine.

However there's a deeper case: what if the resolving job enqueues a job *after* p-limit's `next()` has already run and reported idle? E.g. `limit(() => delay(10).then(() => limit(...)))`. The outer promise from `limit(...)` resolves during the `.then`; the enqueued inner job happens in the same microtask chain. Could the outer `next()` run before the inner `limit()` call? Let's trace: `run` awaits `result` where result is the user function's returned promise. The user function returns `delay(10).then(() => limit(inner))`. The `.then` callback enqueues inner, so result resolves after the enqueue. Thus `next()` runs after inner is queued. Good.

What if the user enqueues in a detached `.then` not part of the returned promise? That's genuinely not tied to the job; the requirement says "resolving a job that enqueues another job" — the standard interpretation is within the job. Our check counts the queue at `next()` time, so anything enqueued before the job's returned promise resolves is counted. That satisfies the requirement.

# p-limit

> Run multiple promise-returning & async functions with limited concurrency

*Works in Node.js and browsers.*

## Install

```sh
npm install p-limit
```

## Usage

```js
import pLimit from 'p-limit';

const limit = pLimit(1);

const input = [
	limit(() => fetchSomething('foo')),
	limit(() => fetchSomething('bar')),
	limit(() => doSomething())
];

// Only one promise is run at once
const result = await Promise.all(input);
console.log(result);
```

## API

### pLimit(concurrency) <sup>default export</sup>

Returns a `limit` function.

#### concurrency

Type: `number | object`\
Minimum: `1`

Concurrency limit.

You can pass a number or an options object with a `concurrency` property.

#### rejectOnClear

Type: `boolean`\
Default: `false`

Reject pending promises with an `AbortError` when `clearQueue()` is called.
This is recommended if you await the returned promises, for example with `Promise.all`, so pending tasks do not remain unresolved after `clearQueue()`.

```js
import pLimit from 'p-limit';

const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1});
```

### limit(fn, ...args)

Returns the promise returned by calling `fn(...args)`.

#### fn

Type: `Function`

Promise-returning/async function.

#### args

Any arguments to pass through to `fn`.

Support for passing arguments on to the `fn` is provided in order to be able to avoid creating unnecessary closures. You probably don't need this optimization unless you're pushing a *lot* of functions.

Warning: Avoid calling the same `limit` function inside a function that is already limited by it. This can create a deadlock where inner tasks never run. Use a separate limiter for inner tasks.

### limit.map(iterable, mapperFunction)

Process an iterable of inputs with limited concurrency.

The mapper function receives the item value and its index.

Returns a promise equivalent to `Promise.all(Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index)))`.

If the iterable throws during iteration, the returned promise rejects with that error. Mapper functions that were already scheduled still run, and their results are discarded.

This is a convenience function for processing inputs that arrive in batches. For more complex use cases, see [p-map](https://github.com/sindresorhus/p-map).

### limit.activeCount

The number of promises that are currently running.

### limit.pendingCount

The number of promises that are waiting to run (i.e. their internal `fn` was not called yet).

### limit.clearQueue()

Discard pending promises that are waiting to run.

This might be useful if you want to tear down the queue at the end of your program's lifecycle or discard any function calls referencing an intermediary state of your app.

Note: This does not cancel promises that are already running.

When `rejectOnClear` is enabled, pending promises are rejected with an `AbortError`.
This is recommended if you await the returned promises, for example with `Promise.all`, so pending tasks do not remain unresolved after `clearQueue()`.

### limit.onIdle()

Returns a promise that resolves when all running promises have settled and the queue is empty.

If the limiter is already idle, the returned promise resolves immediately.

Reserved slots count as active, and a task that enqueues another task is not considered idle until the newly enqueued task also finishes.

```js
import pLimit from 'p-limit';

const limit = pLimit(1);

limit(() => doSomething());
limit(() => doSomethingElse());

await limit.onIdle();
// All tasks have finished
```

### limit.concurrency

Get or set the concurrency limit.

### limitFunction(fn, options) <sup>named export</sup>

Returns a function with limited concurrency.

The returned function manages its own concurrent executions, allowing you to call it multiple times without exceeding the specified concurrency limit.

Ideal for scenarios where you need to control the number of simultaneous executions of a single function, rather than managing concurrency across multiple functions.

```js
import {limitFunction} from 'p-limit';

const limitedFunction = limitFunction(async () => {
	return doSomething();
}, {concurrency: 1});

const input = Array.from({length: 10}, limitedFunction);

// Only one promise is run at once.
await Promise.all(input);
```

#### fn

Type: `Function`

Promise-returning/async function.

#### options

Type: `object`

#### concurrency

Type: `number`\
Minimum: `1`

Concurrency limit.

#### rejectOnClear

Type: `boolean`\
Default: `false`

Reject pending promises with an `AbortError` when `clearQueue()` is called.
This is recommended if you await the returned promises, for example with `Promise.all`, so pending tasks do not remain unresolved after `clearQueue()`.

### limitedFunction.clearQueue()

Discard pending calls that have not started yet.

When `rejectOnClear` is enabled, pending promises are rejected with an `AbortError`. Otherwise, their promises remain unresolved.

This does not cancel calls that are already running.

### limitedFunction.onIdle()

Returns a promise that resolves when all running calls have settled and no calls are pending.

If the function is already idle, the returned promise resolves immediately.

## FAQ

### How is this different from the [`p-queue`](https://github.com/sindresorhus/p-queue) package?

[lines 1-200 of 210]

This package is only about limiting the number of concurrent executions, while `p-queue` is a fully featured queue implementation with lots of different options, introspection, and ability to pause the queue.
